47.6 THE ULTIMATE SPEED
We saw in example (47.4) that even if we continue
to apply a force on a particle for a long time, its speed
cannot exceed c. This is a very general result in special
relativity. In fact, no information can be sent with a
speed greater than c. If we assume that information
can be sent with a speed greater than c, it turns out
that we shall have frames in which a bullet will hit
the bird before it is actually fired, a dog can die before
it is born and so on. If the effect cannot precede its
cause in any frame, then c is the ultimate speed for
any material particle or information.
Scientists have worked out the mathematics for a
world in which all the particles are moving with
respect to each other with speeds greater than c. Such
a world can exist without violating the postulates of
relativity but these particles can never be slowed down
to a speed less than c. The particles of this hypothetical
world cannot interact with ours and in that world,
effect will always precede its cause. Such particles are
named tachyons and a group of physicists is working
to explore the possibility of the actual existence of such
particles. These large speeds and the unworldly results
remind us of several stories from Indian Scriptures
and no wonder the idea of tachyons was mooted by an
Indian scientist E.C.G. Sudarshan.
topics.our_understanding:
So far in our study of special relativity, we have discovered something truly remarkable: the speed of light, which we call c, is not just the fastest thing we know about — it is the absolute speed limit of the universe. No matter how hard you push a particle, no matter how long you keep applying a force, you can never get it to reach or exceed the speed of light. You can get closer and closer, but you will never quite get there. This is not a limitation of our technology — it is a fundamental law of nature baked into the fabric of space and time.

Now, why is this such a big deal? Well, think about what it would mean if information could travel faster than light. Imagine you could send a signal faster than c. It turns out that in some reference frames — remember, different observers moving at different speeds can disagree about the order of events — that signal would appear to arrive before it was even sent. You would have effects happening before their causes. A bullet would hit a bird before the gun was fired. A dog would die before it was even born. That is not just strange — it completely breaks the logical structure of cause and effect that all of physics, and really all of science, depends on. So to protect causality, the principle that causes must always come before their effects, c must be the ultimate speed limit.

Now here is a fascinating twist. Physicists have actually explored the mathematics of a hypothetical world where particles always travel faster than light. These imaginary particles are called tachyons. In their world, they can never slow down to below the speed of light — just as we can never speed up to reach it. The strange thing is, in the tachyon world, effects would always come before causes. Their world and ours can never interact. Tachyons remain purely theoretical, but the idea itself is a beautiful example of how pushing the boundaries of a theory can reveal deep truths. Interestingly, the concept of tachyons was first seriously proposed by the Indian physicist E.C.G. Sudarshan, showing that great physics ideas come from every corner of the world.
examples: Imagine you are pushing a toy car and you keep pushing it harder and harder. At everyday speeds, it keeps getting faster. But if that car were a subatomic particle, something strange would happen as it approached the speed of light. Instead of going faster, the particle would become harder and harder to accelerate — as if it were getting heavier. You could push forever and it would keep getting closer to the speed of light, but it would never actually reach it. It is like trying to reach the horizon — no matter how far you walk, it stays ahead of you.

Think about cause and effect in your daily life. You strike a match, and then the flame appears. The striking is the cause, the flame is the effect. The effect always comes after the cause. Now imagine if a signal could travel faster than light. In some moving reference frames, the math of relativity tells us the signal would appear to arrive at its destination before it left its source. That means the effect would come before the cause — the flame would appear before you struck the match. This is logically impossible, and it is exactly why nothing carrying information can travel faster than light.

Tachyons are the ultimate thought experiment in physics. Picture a world that is like a mirror image of ours — instead of particles that can never reach the speed of light from below, tachyons can never slow down to the speed of light from above. They are always faster than light, and they are stuck that way. In their world, cause and effect run backwards compared to ours. Because of this, tachyons could never send us a message or interact with our particles. They are mathematically consistent but physically isolated from everything we can ever touch or measure.

Here is a way to feel the strangeness of faster-than-light information. Suppose your friend is very far away and you want to warn them about something dangerous. If you could send a warning faster than light, relativity tells us there would exist some observer, moving at just the right speed, who would see your friend receive the warning before you even decided to send it. That observer would say the warning caused you to send it — the whole chain of events flips. This is why physicists say that protecting causality and enforcing the speed of light as the ultimate limit are really the same idea.

47.7 TWIN PARADOX
As the postulates of special relativity lead to
results which contradict ‘common sense’, a number of
interesting paradoxes have been floated. We shall
describe one of the most famous paradoxes of
relativity—the twin paradox. Consider the twins Ram
and Balram living happily on the earth. Ram decides
to make a trip to a distant planet P, which is at rest
with respect to the earth, and come back. He boards
a spaceship S1, going towards the planet with a
uniform velocity. When he reaches the planet, he
jumps from the spaceship S1 to another spaceship S2
which is going towards the earth. When he reaches
the earth, he jumps out and meets his brother Balram.
As Ram returns from his trip and stands next to
Balram, do they have equal age ? Or is Ram younger
than Balram or is he older than Balram ?

following data:

speed of S2 with respect to earth = 0.8c.
When we said that the distance between the earth
and the planet P is 8 light-years, was it clear to you
that this length is the length as measured from the
earth frame ?

view of Balram who is on the earth. For him, both the
spaceships move at a speed 0.8c. So,

The observation of Balram is quite consistent with
the special theory of relativity. Such experiments are
indeed performed in laboratories with radioactive
particles. Particles are accelerated to large speeds and
are kept at these speeds for quite some time by
magnetic fields. These particles with large speeds have
longer lives than their counterparts kept at rest in the
laboratory.
The paradox arises when we analyse the events
from the point of veiw of Ram. When he is in the
spaceship S1, to him the distance between the earth
and the planet is not 8 light-years. The earth and the
planet P are moving with respect to Ram and hence
he is measuring contracted length. The separation is,
therefore, 8 light-years × 0.6 = 4.8 light-years. As the
planet is approaching Ram at 0.8c, the time taken by
the planet to reach Ram is 4.8 light-year/0.8c = 6 years.
So according to Ram’s clock, he jumped from S1 to S2
6 years after getting into S1. Once he is on S2, the
earth and the planet are again moving with the same
speed 0.8c. Again, the earth is 4.8 light-years from the
planet and is approaching at 0.8c. It takes 6 years for
the earth to reach Ram. Thus, according to Ram’s
clock, he was out for 12 years from the earth, the same
result as Balram had expected.
But how about Ram’s calculation of Balram’s age ?
When Ram is on S1, the earth is going away from him

Balram is aging slower than he is. The same is true

on Ram’s clock, he calculates that Balram’s clocks have
advanced only by 12 years × 0.6 = 7.2 years in this
period. According to this analysis, Ram should find
that Balram is 12 – 7.2 = 4.8 years younger than him.
This is the paradox. According to Ram, Balram’s
clocks are running slow and according to Balram,
Ram’s clocks are running slow. Each thinks the other
is younger. Where lies the fallacy ?
The fallacy lies in the fact that Ram has changed
frames whereas Balram has stayed in an inertial
frame. Thus, the roles of the twins are not
symmetrical. The ordering of events are different in
different frames and Ram must take that into account
when he changes frames. Suppose Ram gets into  the
spaceship S1 when his clock reads zero. So does
Balram’s clock. What is the reading of the planet’s
clock at this instant ? According to Balram, it is zero
because both the earth and the planet are at rest and
the clocks are synchronized in his frame. But that is
not so in S1. As Ram gets into S1, he may have the
following conversation with the captain of the ship.
Captain: Welcome aboard S1. I saw you on the
earth, coming towards us. Your jump to board this ship
was perfect. Where are you going ?
Ram: Thank you. I am going to the planet P. How
far is it from here and how long will it take for the
planet to come to us ?
Captain: Planet P is 4.8 light-years from us at the
moment. It is coming towards us at a speed of 0.8c so
it will take 4.8 light-years/0.8c = 6 years for the planet
P to reach us.
Ram: Well, the clocks on the earth and the planet
are running a bit slower than ours. I have been taught
that moving clocks run slow by a factor of γ. This factor
is 1/0.6 for these clocks. So they will advance by 6 years
× 0.6 = 3.6 years by the time the planet reaches us.
Captain: Yes, both the clocks will advance by 3.6
years by the time you jump on the planet P.
Ram: The earth-clock was reading t = 0 as we
passed the earth. This means when I jump on the
planet P the clocks on the earth and the planet will
be reading 3.6 years.
Captain: Here you are mistaken. Don’t you
remember that the planet’s clock is not synchronized
with the earth’s clock ? The planet’s clock is at the rear
end, and hence is running 6.4 years ahead of the
earth’s clock. At the instant the earth’s clock was
reading zero, the planet’s clock was reading 6.4 years.
As the planet reaches us, both the clocks will advance
by 3.6 years. So when you jump out of S1, the earth’s
clock will be reading 3.6 years but the planet’s clock
will be reading 10 years.
Ram understands the logic. In the earth’s frame,
the two clocks read zero simultaneously. But in
S1-frame, the event “planet’s clock reading zero”
occurred several years before “earth’s clock reading
zero”. Six years pass in S1 and Ram finds that the
planet P has reached him. He finds another spaceship
S2 which is heading towards the earth. Ram jumps onto
S2. In the process he looks at the planet’s clock and
finds that it is reading 10 years as calculated by him
on S1. On S2, he starts talking to the commander of the
ship.
Commander: Welcome to S2. How long will you be
with us ?
Ram: Thank you. I am going to Earth. Earth is at
present 4.8 light-years from here and is coming
towards us with a speed of 0.8c. So I will be with you
for 6 years. The captain of S1 told me that the earth’s
clock is reading 3.6 years at this moment whereas the
planet’s clock reads 10 years. There is a difference of
6.4 years in the reading because the two clocks are not
synchronized. Also ….
Commander: Sorry for interrupting you, but you
are mistaken. It is true that the earth’s clock and the
planet’s clock are not synchronized as they are moving
past us. Also the difference in the readings of the two
clocks is 6.4 years. But the planet’s clock is at the front
and the earth’s clock is at the rear. It is the earth’s
clock that is leading by 6.4 years. At the moment the
planet’s clock reads 10 years and hence the earth’s
clock must be reading 16.4 years.
Ram: Hmm… you are right. In S1, the earth was
at the front and its clock lagged behind the planet’s
clock. But in S2 it is the other way round. Indeed the
earth’s clock reads 16.4 years whereas the planet’s
clock reads 10 years.
Commander: That’s right. The earth’s clock is
reading 16.4 years at present. It will advance by another
3.6 years during the 6 years you will be with us. So it
will be reading 20 years when the earth reaches you.
We see that the paradox is resolved.

topics.our_understanding:
Alright, let us talk about one of the most famous puzzles in all of physics — the twin paradox. Imagine two identical twins, Ram and Balram. Ram hops on a spaceship and zooms off to a distant planet, then turns around and comes back. The question is: when they meet again, are they the same age? And here is where it gets really interesting.

From Balram's point of view, sitting comfortably on Earth, Ram is the one who is moving. Because of time dilation — the fact that moving clocks run slow — Ram's heartbeat, his breathing, every biological process in his body ticks at a slower rate. Balram calculates that the round trip takes him twenty years on Earth, but Ram only experiences twelve years. So Ram comes back noticeably younger. This is not a trick or an illusion — Ram genuinely has fewer grey hairs.

Now here is where the so-called paradox creeps in. When Ram is on his spaceship, he could argue that from his perspective, it is Balram and the Earth that are moving away. So shouldn't Balram's clock be the one running slow? If you follow that logic, Ram would predict that Balram aged only about seven years, making Balram the younger one. Both twins can't be younger than the other — that's the contradiction.

The resolution is subtle but beautiful. The situation is not symmetric. Balram stays in a single inertial frame the whole time — he never accelerates, never changes direction. Ram, on the other hand, has to switch from one spaceship to another at the planet, which means he changes his frame of reference mid-journey. When Ram switches ships, there is a sudden jump in what he considers to be 'now' back on Earth. The planet's clock and Earth's clock are not synchronized in Ram's moving frame, and this offset — about six and a half years — is exactly what accounts for the missing time. When you carefully track the clock readings through both legs of the journey, everything adds up perfectly: Balram has aged twenty years, Ram has aged twelve years, and the paradox disappears. The key lesson is that you cannot simply swap the roles of the two twins, because one of them changed inertial frames and the other did not.
examples: Think about radioactive particles called pions created in a particle accelerator. In the lab, these particles are moving at nearly the speed of light, and scientists observe that they live much longer than pions sitting at rest. A pion at rest might decay in a tiny fraction of a second, but a fast-moving pion survives long enough to travel several metres across the detector. This is exactly the twin paradox in action — the moving pion is like Ram on the spaceship, aging more slowly. Its internal clock, which governs when it decays, is genuinely running slow from the lab's perspective.

Imagine you and your best friend both start stopwatches at the same moment. You sit still, and your friend runs a lap around the school field and comes back. In everyday life, both watches read the same time because the speeds involved are tiny. But if your friend could run at eighty percent the speed of light, their watch would read less time than yours when they returned. This is not a malfunction — their watch was genuinely ticking slower the whole time they were moving. Ram's body is just a very complicated biological clock, and it too ran slow during his journey.

Here is the key to resolving the paradox. Suppose you are on a train moving east, and you see two clocks — one at the front of the train and one at the back. Even if those clocks were perfectly synchronized when the train was at rest, once the train is moving, they appear out of sync to you. The front clock seems to lag behind the rear clock. Now when Ram switches from one spaceship to another at the planet, he is essentially jumping from a train going one direction to a train going the opposite direction. The clock he sees on Earth suddenly jumps forward by about six and a half years in his new frame. That jump is real, and it is exactly what makes the total age difference work out correctly.

Scientists have actually tested this with real clocks on aeroplanes. In the nineteen seventies, very precise atomic clocks were flown around the world on jet planes while identical clocks stayed on the ground. When the planes landed, the clocks that had been flying showed slightly less elapsed time than the ground clocks. The effect was tiny — just billionths of a second — because aeroplanes move nowhere near the speed of light. But the difference was real and matched the predictions of relativity perfectly. Ram's situation is just a much more dramatic version of the same effect.

How is that even possible? <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:the_special_theory_of_relativity:47_7:spacetime_twin>> Here is our cast. Balram stays on Earth — perfectly still, perfectly comfortable. That's 10 years each way — 20 years total for Balram. Ram moves at 0.8c, so his clock runs at a fraction of Balram's rate — specifically, the Lorentz factor gamma tells us how much slower. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 - 0.64}} = \frac{1}{0.6}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:ram-leg1>> Now — time dilation. questions.q_text: A scientist is riding a perfectly smooth train moving at constant speed. She drops a ball straight down and watches it fall. What does she observe, and what does this tell her about her motion?
options: A. The ball falls slightly backward, revealing that the train is moving forward.
B. The ball falls straight down, exactly as it would if she were standing still — she cannot tell she is moving from this experiment alone.
C. The ball falls straight down, but this only works because gravity cancels out the train's motion.
D. The ball falls slightly forward, because the train is carrying it along.

questions.q_text: According to the principle of relativity, which of the following statements is correct about two observers moving at constant velocity relative to each other?
options: A. The observer who is truly at rest will measure slightly different results in mechanical experiments than the moving observer.
B. Only one observer can be considered truly at rest — the one who is not moving relative to the Earth.
C. Neither observer is more 'at rest' than the other — both frames are equally valid for describing mechanical experiments.
D. The principle only applies when both observers are moving at the same speed.

questions.q_text: You are on a smooth airplane flying at a constant 900 kilometers per hour. Your friend claims you could figure out the plane's speed by carefully measuring how a ball rolls across a flat table inside the cabin. Is your friend right?
options: A. Yes — the ball will roll slightly backward because the plane is moving forward, revealing the plane's speed.
B. No — because the plane is an inertial frame, no mechanical experiment inside the cabin can reveal its speed relative to the ground.
C. Yes — but only if the table is perfectly level and there is no air resistance.
D. No — but only because the plane's speed is too slow for the effect to be noticeable.

questions.q_text: Two spaceships, Alpha and Beta, are far from any planets. From Alpha's perspective, Beta is drifting past at a steady 500 kilometers per second. The pilot of Alpha says she is at rest and Beta is moving. The pilot of Beta says he is at rest and Alpha is moving. A student argues that one of them must be wrong — only one ship can truly be at rest. Using the principle of relativity, explain clearly why the student is mistaken, and what 'motion is relative' actually means here.
questions.answer: Step 1 — Identify what the principle of relativity says. The principle states that there is no preferred inertial frame of reference. No frame is more 'truly at rest' than any other. Any observer in a non-accelerating frame can legitimately consider themselves to be at rest. Step 2 — Apply this to the two spaceships. Both Alpha and Beta are moving at constant velocity relative to each other — neither is accelerating. This means both are valid inertial frames. Alpha's pilot saying 'I am at rest and Beta moves past me at 500 km/s' is a perfectly valid description. Beta's pilot saying 'I am at rest and Alpha moves past me at 500 km/s' is equally valid. Step 3 — Address the student's objection. The student assumes there is some absolute, cosmic sense of 'being at rest' — like a universal scoreboard. But the principle of relativity tells us no such thing exists. There is no experiment either pilot can perform inside their own ship (using mechanics) that would prove they are the one truly moving. Step 4 — State the conclusion. 'Motion is relative' means that speed and rest only have meaning when you specify relative to what. Alpha is at rest relative to itself, and moving relative to Beta. Beta is at rest relative to itself, and moving relative to Alpha. Both statements are simultaneously true and equally valid. The student is wrong because they are assuming absolute motion exists — but it does not.

questions.q_text: The explanation describes a tension that troubled physicists before Einstein. What was that tension, and why was it a problem for the principle of relativity?
options: A. Newton's laws gave different predictions depending on how fast an object was moving, which contradicted the idea of consistent physics across frames.

B. The laws of electricity and magnetism appeared to single out one special frame of reference, meaning an electrical experiment might reveal absolute motion — which would violate the principle of relativity.
C. Gravity was found to behave differently on moving trains than on stationary platforms, undermining Newton's laws.
D. The principle of relativity worked for electricity and magnetism but broke down for mechanical experiments at high speeds.

B. One and a half times the speed of light, because B's motion adds to the light's speed

B. It found no difference at all in light's speed in any direction, suggesting that motion through space cannot be detected using light

D. It found that the speed of light depends on the colour of the light used

B. Because the light pulse is measured to be the same distance from both observers simultaneously, even though the observers are not in the same place
C. Because one observer is moving and therefore cannot make accurate measurements
D. Because the speed of light changes slightly depending on how fast the observer is moving

B. First, the laws of nature look identical in all inertial frames; second, the speed of light in vacuum is the same for every observer
C. First, no object can reach the speed of light; second, moving clocks run slower than stationary ones
D. First, electricity and magnetism are the same force; second, light is an electromagnetic wave

questions.q_text: Observer A stands on a platform. Observer B is on a train moving away from A at a very high constant speed. At the moment they are side by side, a light pulse is fired in the direction the train is moving. After a short time, A measures the light to be 300 metres away from A. B also measures the light to be 300 metres away from B. But A and B are no longer in the same place — B has moved, say, 150 metres down the track from A. How can the light be 300 metres from A and also 300 metres from B at the same moment, if A and B are 150 metres apart? What must this tell us about time or distance for the two observers?
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Identify the contradiction with ordinary arithmetic. In everyday life, if the light is 300 metres from A, and B is 150 metres ahead of A in the same direction, then the light should be only 150 metres from B. That is how distances normally subtract. But the experiment tells us the light is 300 metres from B as well. This is a genuine contradiction with ordinary arithmetic.

Step 2 — Recognise that both measurements cannot be simultaneously true unless something is different about how A and B experience space or time. The only way both measurements can be correct is if the metre sticks or clocks used by A and B are not equivalent. Either B's metre stick is shorter than A's (length contraction), or B's clock is ticking at a different rate than A's (time dilation), or both.

Step 3 — Interpret the physical meaning. The phrase 'at the same moment' is itself the problem. Special relativity tells us that two events that appear simultaneous to A may not appear simultaneous to B. The concept of 'at the same time' is not absolute — it depends on the observer's state of motion.

Step 4 — State the conclusion. The constancy of the speed of light for all observers forces us to abandon the idea that time and distance are the same for everyone. Moving observers experience time passing at a different rate and measure distances differently compared to stationary observers. This is not an illusion or a measurement error — it is a fundamental feature of reality, confirmed by experiments such as the behaviour of fast-moving particles in accelerators and the corrections needed for GPS satellites.

B. The astronaut's watch measures the proper time because it is present at both events, and proper time is always the shortest measured interval.
C. The Earth clocks measure the proper time because Earth is the larger and more important reference frame.
D. Both measurements are equally proper, so neither six hours nor eight hours is more correct than the other.

A second observer is on a train moving toward one end of the box. What does the train observer conclude about when the light reaches each end?
options: A. The train observer also sees the light reach both ends simultaneously, because the speed of light is the same for everyone.
B. The train observer sees the light reach the far end first, because that end is running away from the light pulse.
C. The train observer sees the light reach the near end first, because that end is moving toward the light pulse.
D. The train observer cannot make any judgment because they are not in the same frame as the box.

questions.q_text: A spaceship flies past you at close to the speed of light. In which direction do you observe the spaceship to be contracted, and what length is considered the proper length?

B. Contracted in the direction of motion; the proper length is the length measured by the astronaut inside the ship.
C. Contracted in the direction of motion; the proper length is the length you measure as it passes.
D. Contracted in all directions equally; the proper length is the average of both observers' measurements.

questions.q_text: A light-clock consists of two mirrors separated by a distance of 1.5 metres, with a light pulse bouncing between them. When the clock is at rest, calculate the time for one full round trip of the light pulse. Then explain in words — without calculating gamma — why the same clock ticks more slowly when it moves sideways past you at high speed.
questions.answer: Step 1 — Find the round-trip time when the clock is at rest. The light pulse travels from one mirror to the other and back, covering a total distance of 2 times 1.5 metres, which equals 3 metres. The speed of light is approximately 3 times 10 to the power 8 metres per second. So the time for one tick is: time equals distance divided by speed, which is 3 metres divided by 3 times 10 to the power 8 metres per second, giving 1 times 10 to the power negative 8 seconds, or 10 nanoseconds. Step 2 — Explain why the moving clock ticks more slowly. When the clock moves sideways past you, the light pulse no longer travels straight up and down from your point of view. Instead, it must travel a longer, diagonal path — going sideways with the clock while also going up and down between the mirrors. The total distance the light covers in one round trip is therefore greater than 3 metres as you observe it. Since the second postulate of special relativity tells us the speed of light is exactly the same for all observers regardless of motion, and since speed equals distance divided by time, a longer distance at the same speed means a longer time. The clock therefore takes more time to complete each tick as seen by you — it runs slow. The clock's own rest frame still measures 10 nanoseconds per tick, which is the proper time. You measure a longer, improper time interval for the same two events.

B. Gamma is approximately one, so relativistic momentum is approximately equal to rest mass times velocity.
C. Gamma is approximately zero, so relativistic momentum is nearly zero regardless of velocity.
D. Gamma is approximately one, but relativistic momentum is still infinite because light speed is involved.

options: A. The force gradually weakens over time because the particle moves away from its source.
B. The particle runs out of internal energy and can no longer accelerate.
C. As the particle speeds up, its effective mass grows without limit, so each push produces less and less additional speed, requiring infinite force to reach light speed.
D. The speed of light is only unreachable in practice due to engineering limits, not because of any fundamental law.

questions.q_text: An astronaut is traveling on a spaceship moving at 90 percent of the speed of light relative to Earth. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: A. The astronaut feels heavier than normal and notices their own mass has increased.
B. The astronaut's rest mass is unchanged from their own perspective, but an Earth observer measures a larger effective mass for the astronaut.
C. Both the astronaut and the Earth observer agree that the astronaut's mass has increased.

questions.q_text: In relativistic dynamics, as a particle's speed approaches the speed of light, what happens to its momentum?
options: A. Momentum approaches a fixed maximum value equal to rest mass times the speed of light.
B. Momentum decreases because the particle's acceleration drops to zero.
C. Momentum grows without limit, since the gamma factor increases without bound.
D. Momentum stays constant once the particle reaches 99 percent of light speed.

questions.q_text: A particle of rest mass m is initially at rest. A constant force F is applied to it starting at time zero. Using the relativistic result for speed under a constant force, explain what happens to the particle's speed at very early times compared to very late times, and confirm that light speed is never reached.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Write down the relativistic speed formula. The speed at time t is given by: speed equals (F times t divided by m) all divided by the square root of one plus (F times t divided by m times c) squared, where c is the speed of light. We can write the ratio F times t divided by m times c as a dimensionless quantity — call it R. So speed equals R times c divided by the square root of one plus R squared.

Step 2 — Check early times (R is very small, much less than one). When R is tiny, the square root of one plus R squared is approximately one. So speed is approximately R times c, which equals F times t divided by m. This is exactly Newton's second law: force equals mass times acceleration, giving speed proportional to time. Relativity reduces to Newton at low speeds, as expected.

Step 3 — Check late times (R grows very large). When R is huge, the square root of one plus R squared is approximately equal to R itself (since R squared dominates the one). So speed approaches R times c divided by R, which equals c. The speed approaches the speed of light but never equals it, because the square root is always slightly larger than R — it equals the square root of R squared plus one, which is always greater than R.

Step 4 — Confirm light speed is unreachable. For the speed to equal c exactly, we would need R divided by the square root of one plus R squared to equal one. That would require one plus R squared to equal R squared, meaning one equals zero — which is impossible. Therefore, no finite force applied for any finite time can bring the particle to light speed. The mathematics guarantees it.

questions.q_text: A small metal bead has a rest mass of 2 grams. If every bit of its mass could be completely converted into pure energy, how much energy would be released? The speed of light is 300 million metres per second. Show your reasoning clearly.
questions.answer:
Step 1 — Write down what we know. The rest mass is 2 grams, which we must convert to kilograms: 2 grams equals 0.002 kilograms. The speed of light is 300 million metres per second, which is 3 times 10 to the power 8 metres per second.

Step 2 — Apply the rest mass energy formula. Energy equals mass times the speed of light squared. So we calculate: Energy equals 0.002 multiplied by (3 times 10 to the power 8) squared.

Step 3 — Square the speed of light. (3 times 10 to the power 8) squared equals 9 times 10 to the power 16 metres squared per second squared.

Step 4 — Multiply. Energy equals 0.002 times 9 times 10 to the power 16, which equals 1.8 times 10 to the power 14 joules.

Step 5 — Interpret the result. That is 180 trillion joules — roughly twice the energy from the one-gram paperclip example in the text, which makes sense because we have twice the mass. This enormous figure illustrates why even a tiny mass holds a staggering amount of energy locked inside it.

B. Its total energy equals its momentum multiplied by the speed of light

questions.q_text: Suppose a scientist claims to have invented a device that sends a warning signal faster than light. A friend 10 light-minutes away receives the warning. Explain, step by step, why this device would threaten the principle of causality, and what a moving observer might conclude about the order of events.
questions.answer: Step 1 — Understand the setup. The scientist sends a signal that travels faster than light. The friend receives it 10 light-minutes away. In the scientist's own reference frame, the signal is sent first and received second — cause before effect, as normal. Step 2 — Introduce a moving observer. Special relativity tells us that different observers moving at different velocities can disagree about the timing of events that are separated in space. For a signal traveling faster than light, the mathematics of the Lorentz transformation shows that there exists some observer moving at just the right velocity who would calculate that the signal arrived at the friend's location before it left the scientist's device. Step 3 — Identify the causality violation. For that moving observer, the effect (the friend receiving the warning) happens before the cause (the scientist sending it). This observer might even conclude that receiving the warning is what caused the scientist to send it — the entire logical chain of cause and effect is reversed. Step 4 — State the conclusion. Because faster-than-light signaling leads to situations where effects precede causes depending on the observer's frame of motion, it is logically incompatible with a consistent universe. Causality — the rule that causes must always come before their effects — would be violated. This is why physicists treat the speed of light as an absolute upper limit for any signal carrying information, not merely a practical engineering barrier.

questions.q_text: Ram travels to a distant planet and back. Balram, who stays on Earth, ages twenty years during the round trip. Ram ages only twelve years. Ram argues that from his perspective on the outbound leg, Balram's clock was running slow, and on the inbound leg, Balram's clock was also running slow. He calculates that Balram aged only about seven years across both legs combined. Yet we know Balram actually aged twenty years. Identify the source of the missing thirteen years in Ram's accounting, and explain why Ram's simple calculation is wrong.
questions.answer: Step 1 — Identify what Ram's calculation includes. On the outbound leg, Ram correctly notes that Balram's clock appears to run slow from his moving frame. On the inbound leg, Ram again correctly notes that Balram's clock appears to run slow. Adding these two contributions gives roughly seven years for Balram — far less than twenty. So Ram is missing about thirteen years in his accounting. Step 2 — Identify what Ram's calculation leaves out. Ram's calculation ignores what happens at the turnaround point at the planet. When Ram switches from the outbound spaceship to the inbound spaceship, he changes his inertial frame. In his new inertial frame, the clocks on Earth and the planet are synchronized differently than they were in his old frame. Specifically, Earth's clock reading jumps forward by approximately six and a half years in Ram's new frame the moment he switches ships. Step 3 — Reconstruct the full accounting. Outbound leg: Balram ages roughly three and a half years according to Ram's frame. Turnaround: Earth's clock jumps forward by about thirteen years in Ram's new frame (the exact value that closes the gap). Inbound leg: Balram ages roughly three and a half years again according to Ram's frame. Total for Balram: three and a half plus thirteen plus three and a half equals twenty years. This matches perfectly. Step 4 — State the key lesson. Ram's simple calculation was wrong because he treated his two inertial frames as if they were one continuous frame. The jump in Earth's clock reading at the turnaround is a real, calculable effect of switching frames, not a trick. It is precisely this jump that breaks the apparent symmetry and resolves the paradox. Balram aged twenty years, Ram aged twelve years, and the difference is fully accounted for.

B. The size of the effect depends on the speed involved; jet planes move far slower than light, so the effect is tiny but real and matches relativity's predictions exactly
C. The result was actually caused by air pressure differences at altitude, not by time dilation
D. The twin paradox only applies when one traveller changes direction, and planes flying in a circle do not count
